lessons.title: und, oder, aber: join two sentences at work
lessons.goal: Name things in the office and join two sentences with und, oder and aber.

grammar.point: und, oder and aber join two full sentences; they sit on chair 0, so the word order after them does not change
grammar.oneLine: Ich bin müde, aber ich muss arbeiten. aber is chair 0: then ich, then the verb.

mistake.wrong: Ich bin müde, aber muss ich arbeiten.
mistake.right: Ich bin müde, aber ich muss arbeiten.
mistake.why: aber does not count as a part. It sits on chair 0, so the second sentence starts normally: ich on chair 1, the verb on chair 2.

terms.meaning: a linking word that joins two sentences, like und (and), oder (or), aber (but)
a full sentence with its own subject and its own verb in position 2
a seat in front of chair 1; a word there does not count, so the verb stays on chair 2

cards.title: Before we start: joining two sentences
cards.body: Chapter 7 is your working day: the office, tasks in order, how you travel, where you go, polite requests. Today: at work you often say two things at once, like tired but must work. A small word joins two sentences.
steps: You already know: ich bin, ich muss and aber from chapters 1 and 5
New today: und, oder, aber join two full sentences, and the word order after them stays the same
By the end you can: join two thoughts in one sentence, like Ich bin müde, aber ich muss arbeiten

examples.de: Ich bin müde, aber ich muss arbeiten.
examples.en: I am tired, but I have to work.
examples.why: New today: aber joins two sentences. The second one keeps its normal order.

cards.more: Think of two train carriages. Each carriage is a full sentence with its own engine, the verb. Und, oder and aber are the little coupling between them. The coupling does not change the carriages: the second sentence still starts with the person and the verb in second place, just like before. Und adds, oder gives a choice, aber says but. German also puts a comma before aber. You will learn this step by step in the next cards.

cards.title: In the office: das Büro
cards.body: This chapter is about a working day. First the office words. Learn each with der, die or das and the plural. im Büro means in the office: learn it as one piece. Why it is im comes in lesson 7.

examples.why: im Büro is one piece for now.

cards.more: Picture your desk at work. Every thing on it has a little name tag: der, die or das. Step 1: say the article and the noun together, like der Drucker. Step 2: add the plural: die Drucker (no change, like der Computer). Step 3: notice die Firma becomes die Firmen. The a turns into en. That is a rare one, so learn it by heart. im Büro is a ready-made piece, like im Supermarkt in chapter 4. Extra example: Die Firma ist klein. = The company is small.
cards.lead: The intro showed how this lesson joins sentences. On this card: the office words you need, each with der, die or das, so you can say what is on your desk.

deeper.text: Long German nouns are often two words glued together. Schreibtisch is Schreib (writing) + Tisch (table). The last part decides the article, so Tisch is der and Schreibtisch is der too. When you meet a long new word, look at its last part first.

cards.title: und: two sentences become one
cards.body: und means and. It can join two whole sentences. Each sentence keeps its own subject and its own verb. Nothing moves. You may put a comma before und, or leave it out.

examples.de: Mira schreibt E-Mails, und Ben telefoniert.
examples.en: Mira writes emails, and Ben is on the phone.

examples.de: Ich habe einen Laptop, und Anna hat einen Computer.
examples.en: I have a laptop, and Anna has a computer.
examples.why: Each part has its own verb.

examples.de: Der Drucker ist alt, und er ist laut.
examples.en: The printer is old, and it is loud.

cards.more: Think of two train cars. Each car is a full sentence with its own engine, the verb. und is the little hook between them. The hook does not go inside a car, so nothing in the cars moves. Step 1: say sentence one. Step 2: say und. Step 3: say sentence two exactly as you would alone. Extra example: Ich arbeite, und Leon schläft. = I work, and Leon sleeps.
cards.lead: You just met the office words. Next: one small word that joins two full sentences, so you can say two things in one breath, like at work.

deeper.text: In English there is usually no comma before and. In German the comma is optional, and many writers add it when the second sentence has its own subject. It shows the reader: a new sentence starts here. Short sentences often skip it. Both are correct.

cards.title: Chair 0: und does not count
cards.body: Remember the chairs: the verb sits on chair 2. und, oder and aber sit on chair 0, in front of everything. So after them, count again from 1. If a time word is on chair 1, the subject moves behind the verb, as always.

examples.de: Heute arbeite ich, und morgen habe ich Zeit.
examples.en: Today I work, and tomorrow I have time.

examples.de: Ich drucke den Plan, und Leon kopiert ihn.
examples.en: I print the plan, and Leon copies it.

examples.de: Anna kommt um acht, und um neun beginnt die Arbeit.
examples.en: Anna comes at eight, and at nine work starts.

cards.more: Imagine a waiting room. Chair 0 is the doorway, not a real seat. und only stands in the doorway. The real chairs start behind it. Step 1: put und in the doorway. Step 2: put someone or a time on chair 1. Step 3: the verb takes chair 2. Step 4: if a time word took chair 1, the subject sits on chair 3. Extra example: Ich bin hier, und morgen bin ich in Berlin. = I am here, and tomorrow I am in Berlin.
cards.lead: You can now join sentences with und. On this card: how word order works after und, oder and aber, so the verb stays in the right place in the second sentence.

deeper.text: Why does the word order not change? Because und is glue, not a part of the sentence. Test it: cover und and the second half still stands alone as a correct sentence. That is always true for und, oder and aber, so you never need to rearrange anything.

example.de: Ich arbeite, und um zehn habe ich Pause.
example.en: I work, and at ten I have a break.

cards.title: oder: a choice
cards.body: oder means or. It gives a choice between two sentences. It also sits on chair 0, so the second sentence keeps its normal order. A question with oder asks: this one or that one?

examples.de: Trinkst du Kaffee, oder möchtest du Tee?
examples.en: Are you drinking coffee, or would you like tea?
examples.why: Two yes/no questions, joined by oder.

examples.de: Wir drucken den Plan, oder wir schreiben eine E-Mail.
examples.en: We print the plan, or we write an email.

examples.de: Arbeitest du heute im Büro, oder arbeitest du zu Hause?
examples.en: Are you working in the office today, or are you working at home?

cards.more: oder is a fork in the road. You stand at the fork and pick one path. Each path is a full sentence. Step 1: say the first option. Step 2: say oder. Step 3: say the second option in its own normal order. In a question, both halves start with the verb. You know oder already from Zusammen oder getrennt? in the café. Extra example: Kommst du mit, oder bleibst du hier? = Are you coming along, or are you staying here?
cards.lead: The card before showed the order after und. Next: oder, which gives a choice, so you can ask whether someone wants tea or coffee.

deeper.text: In speech, oder at the end of a statement works like English "right?" or "isn't it?". You say a sentence and add oder? to check that the other person agrees. It is very common and friendly, and you do not change anything else in the sentence.

cards.title: aber: but, always with a comma
cards.body: aber means but. It shows a contrast: something is different from what you expect. aber also sits on chair 0. Put a comma before aber every time.

examples.de: Ich bin müde, aber ich muss arbeiten.
examples.en: I am tired, but I have to work.
examples.why: aber = 0, ich = 1, muss = 2, arbeiten at the end.

examples.de: Der Drucker ist neu, aber er ist sehr laut.
examples.en: The printer is new, but it is very loud.

examples.de: Ich habe einen Laptop, aber ich habe keinen Drucker.
examples.en: I have a laptop, but I don't have a printer.

steps: Ich bin müde.
Ich muss arbeiten.
Ich bin müde, + aber + ich muss arbeiten.
= Ich bin müde, aber ich muss arbeiten.
cards.more: aber is the word for a surprise turn. You expect one thing, then something else comes. I am tired... so I sleep? No: aber I have to work. Step 1: say sentence one. Step 2: comma and aber. Step 3: say sentence two exactly as it would be alone. The most common mistake is to put the verb right after aber. Do not: aber is only the doorway. Extra example: Die Firma ist klein, aber sie ist gut. = The company is small, but it is good.
cards.lead: Oder gives a choice. On this card: aber, the word for but, so you can say something is different from what you expect, like being tired but still working.

deeper.text: German writes a comma between almost every pair of sentences, where English often skips it. The comma is a written signal: a new sentence begins. When you speak, you hear it as a tiny pause before aber. So for aber the comma is never optional.

example.de: Anna ist müde, aber sie arbeitet.
example.en: Anna is tired, but she is working.

cards.title: Same person twice? Drop the second one
cards.body: If both sentences have the same subject, you may leave the second one out after und or oder. Then the second verb comes right after und. No comma. With aber, keep the subject: it is clearer.

examples.de: Ich stehe früh auf und trinke einen Kaffee.
examples.en: I get up early and drink a coffee.

examples.de: Mira druckt den Plan und kopiert ihn.
examples.en: Mira prints the plan and copies it.

examples.de: Arbeitest du heute oder hast du frei?
examples.en: Are you working today or are you off?

rows: Mira druckt den Plan, und sie kopiert ihn.
Mira druckt den Plan und kopiert ihn.

cards.more: Saying ich twice sounds a bit like a robot: I work and I phone and I print. Germans often say the person once. Step 1: check that both sentences have the same person. Step 2: keep the person only in the first one. Step 3: after und, go straight to the verb, and keep its ending for that person. Careful: in Arbeitest du heute oder hast du frei? the second question still needs du after hast, because it is a question. frei haben = to be off work. Extra example: Ben kocht und isst. = Ben cooks and eats.
cards.lead: Last card of the joining rules: when both sentences have the same subject, you can shorten the second one, so you can say what you do in one smooth sentence.

deeper.text: When two verbs share one subject, both verbs must fit that subject. Ich arbeite und telefoniere: both end in -e because both belong to ich. With wir, both would end in -en. If the two verbs need different endings, you must say both subjects.

lessons.title: A working day: zuerst, dann, danach
lessons.goal: Describe your working day step by step with zuerst, dann and danach.

grammar.point: zuerst, dann and danach are time words: on chair 1 they push the subject behind the verb; after und, dann is chair 1 again
grammar.oneLine: Zuerst lese ich E-Mails, und dann trinke ich Kaffee. Verb on chair 2 every time.

mistake.wrong: Zuerst ich lese E-Mails, und dann ich trinke Kaffee.
mistake.right: Zuerst lese ich E-Mails, und dann trinke ich Kaffee.
mistake.why: zuerst and dann take chair 1. The verb must be on chair 2, so ich moves behind it.

terms.meaning: the order of things: first this, then that
a time word that shows the order: zuerst (first), dann (then), danach (after that)
the end of the working day, the free time after work

cards.title: Before we start: a working day in order
cards.body: Your boss asks: what do you do at work? You want to tell the day in order: first emails, then coffee. Words like zuerst and dann act like the numbers 1, 2, 3 of your day.
steps: You already know: time first, verb second: Heute spiele ich Tennis (chapter 2)
New today: zuerst, dann, danach start the sentence, and the verb still comes second
By the end you can: tell your working day step by step

examples.why: New today: zuerst is the new time word at the start.

examples.de: Ich lese E-Mails, und dann trinke ich Kaffee.
examples.en: I read emails, and then I drink coffee.
examples.why: New today: und dann joins two steps.

cards.more: A day is like a row of little boxes: first, then, after that. In German you stick a small label on each box. The label goes first in the sentence, and the verb stays right behind it, in second place. That is the rule you already used with Am Montag and Heute. The person moves behind the verb. Nothing else is new. You will build this step by step in the next cards.

cards.title: Four words for the order
cards.body: To tell a day step by step, use four time words: zuerst (first), dann (then), danach (after that), später (later). They work like heute or morgen: they say when.

examples.en: After that I take a break.

cards.more: Think of a recipe: first this, then that, after that the next thing. German has the same little signposts. Step 1: zuerst opens the list. Step 2: dann and danach move you forward. You can use them as often as you like. Step 3: später means a bit later. Tip: danach = da + nach, after that. Extra example: Zuerst koche ich, dann esse ich. = First I cook, then I eat.
cards.lead: In the last lesson you joined sentences with und. Next: how to tell a day step by step, so you can say what you do first, then and later.

deeper.text: dann and danach are close cousins. dann is the general then. danach means after that and points back to the step you just named, so it fits best right after something finished. später is vaguer: some time later, without saying when.

cards.title: On chair 1: the verb stays on chair 2
cards.body: zuerst, dann and danach usually start the sentence. Then they sit on chair 1. The verb stays on chair 2, and the subject moves to chair 3. It is the same rule as Am Montag spiele ich.

examples.en: After that we have a meeting.

cards.more: Same chairs as always. The verb owns chair 2 and never gives it away. If zuerst takes chair 1, the person has to sit on chair 3. Step 1: put the sequence word first. Step 2: put the verb right after it. Step 3: then the person. Step 4: the rest. A common mistake is Zuerst ich trinke. That puts the verb on chair 3. Extra example: Danach fahre ich nach Hause. = After that I go home.
cards.lead: You now have four time words for order. On this card: what happens to the verb when one of them starts the sentence, so you can say what you do next.

deeper.text: Why does the subject jump behind the verb? German keeps the verb on chair 2 always, and chair 1 can hold any part. You do not need to memorise a trick. Just ask: what is on chair 1? If it is not the subject, the verb comes next, then the subject.

example.en: After that Leon makes a phone call.

cards.title: und dann: und is chair 0, dann is chair 1
cards.body: You can join two steps with und dann. und sits on chair 0, as you learned. dann sits on chair 1. So the verb comes right after dann, and the subject after the verb.

examples.de: Ich lese E-Mails, und dann trinke ich Kaffee.
examples.en: I read emails, and then I drink coffee.

examples.de: Anna telefoniert, und dann schreibt sie einen Plan.
examples.en: Anna makes a phone call, and then she writes a plan.

examples.de: Wir essen, und danach machen wir Pause.
examples.en: We eat, and after that we take a break.

cards.more: Two small words, two different jobs. und is the doorway (chair 0) and does not count. dann is a real guest: it takes chair 1. So after und dann, the verb must come next. Step 1: say und. Step 2: say dann. Step 3: say the verb. Step 4: say the person. Say it out loud a few times: und dann trinke ich, und dann schreibe ich. It becomes a rhythm. Extra example: Ich esse, und dann schlafe ich. = I eat, and then I sleep.
cards.lead: You can start a sentence with zuerst or dann. Next: joining two steps with und dann, so you can describe a whole morning in one sentence.

deeper.text: und dann is how people tell a story out loud. You will hear it again and again: und dann, und dann. The comma before und is optional. Only the part after dann needs care: verb first, then subject. Nothing else changes.

example.de: Leon liest, und dann schreibt er.
example.en: Leon reads, and then he writes.

cards.title: Tasks at work
cards.body: Here are typical tasks. Most are a verb + an object: E-Mails schreiben, E-Mails beantworten (answer), eine E-Mail schicken (send). Pause machen means to take a break. No article: Ich mache Pause.

examples.en: Frau Weber gets a task done.

cards.more: A working day is a list of jobs. Each job is a little verb + thing pair. Step 1: pick the thing: E-Mails, eine Aufgabe. Step 2: pick the verb: schreiben, beantworten, erledigen. Step 3: give the verb the right ending for the person. beantworten ends in -ten, so it gets the extra e: du beantwortest, er beantwortet, like arbeiten in chapter 2. Extra example: Leon beantwortet E-Mails. = Leon answers emails.
cards.lead: Now you can order a day. Next: the typical office tasks, with verbs like beantworten and schicken, so you can list what you do at work.

deeper.text: Some verb and noun pairs are fixed and have no article: Pause machen, Feierabend haben. You do not say a break or the break. Learn the pair as one piece. English does this too, in phrases like have lunch, so it is not as strange as it looks.

cards.title: Clock times and the end of work
cards.body: Add clock times with um. The day ends with Feierabend: the free time after work. Ich habe um fünf Feierabend. Mittags esse ich in der Kantine (in the canteen): learn it as one piece. Why der comes in lesson 7.

steps: Um acht Uhr fange ich an.

Dann habe ich eine Besprechung.

cards.more: Now your day has a clock. Start and end with times, and fill the middle with zuerst, dann and danach. Step 1: Um acht Uhr fange ich an. anfangen is separable, so an goes to the very end. Step 2: add the steps. Step 3: close with Feierabend. Germans love this word: Feier = party, Abend = evening. It is the moment you leave work. Extra example: Wann hast du Feierabend? – Um sechzehn Uhr. = When do you finish work? – At four pm.
cards.lead: You can name tasks. Next: clock times and the end of the working day, so you can say when work starts and when you finish.

deeper.text: In speech, people usually drop Uhr and say Um fünf, not Um siebzehn Uhr. The 24-hour style with siebzehn is for timetables, work rosters and official notices. Both mean five in the afternoon. Use the short form when you talk.

cards.title: Ask about someone's day
cards.body: Ask with question words and the verb on chair 2: Was machst du zuerst? Wann hast du Feierabend? Wie lange machst du Pause? With a modal, the second verb goes to the end: Was musst du danach machen?

examples.en: After that I have to answer emails.

cards.more: Questions about a day are easy: you already know the question words. Step 1: pick was, wann or wie lange. Step 2: put the verb on chair 2. Step 3: add du. Step 4: answer with the same sequence word first: Zuerst … With müssen the bracket comes back: muss on chair 2, the other verb at the very end. Extra example: Was machst du danach? – Danach fahre ich nach Hause. = What do you do after that? – After that I go home.
cards.lead: Last card of this lesson: asking about someone's day, so you can ask what a colleague does first and when they finish.

deeper.text: A question with a question word follows the same rule as a statement: the verb is on chair 2. Chair 1 holds Was, Wann or Wie lange. Wie lange is two words but counts as one part: how long. A yes/no question has no question word, so the verb comes first.

lessons.goal: Understand why it is mit dem Bus and say with whom and how you go to work.

grammar.point: mit is always followed by the dative: der → dem, das → dem, die → der, plural die → den + -n on the noun
grammar.oneLine: mit dem Chef, mit dem Team, mit der Chefin, mit den Kindern. After mit: dem, der, dem, den + n.

mistake.why: mit always takes the dative. In the dative, die (feminine) becomes der.

terms.meaning: a third form of the article (after nominative and accusative); you use it after some little words like mit
the form a noun group takes for its job: nominative (subject), accusative (object), dative (after mit and others)
the dative of wer: Mit wem? = with whom?

cards.title: Before we start: why it is mit dem Bus
cards.body: You already say mit dem Bus in Hamburg. Today you find out why dem, and why mit der U-Bahn changes the little word. Then you can say how you go to work and with whom you work.
steps: You already know: mit dem Bus as one piece (chapter 3), and den for objects (chapter 4)
New today: after mit, the little word changes: der and das become dem, die becomes der
By the end you can: say how you go to work and with whom you work

examples.why: You know this already. You learned mit dem Bus as one piece.
New today: die U-Bahn becomes der U-Bahn after mit.

examples.en: I am talking to the boss.
examples.why: New today: mit dem works with people too.

cards.more: In chapter 4, the word der changed to den when the noun was an object. Today a second job for the little word: some small words, like mit, make it change in a new way. This new form is called the dative. It is just another costume for der, die, das. You already wear it in mit dem Bus. You will learn this step by step in the next cards, one gender at a time.

cards.title: Now the secret: why mit dem Bus?
cards.body: In chapter 3 you learned mit dem Bus and mit der U-Bahn as pieces. Here is why. mit always makes the next article change. This new form is called the dative. It is a third form, after the nominative and the accusative.
cards.more: You already know two outfits for an article. The nominative is the everyday outfit: der Bus. The accusative is the object outfit: den Bus. Now there is a third outfit: the dative. mit is like a door with a dress code: everyone who walks through it must wear the dative outfit. Step 1: see mit. Step 2: switch to the dative. Step 3: say the noun as normal. Extra example: Ich fahre mit dem Zug. = I go by train.
cards.lead: In chapter 3 you said mit dem Bus as a piece. Next: why the article changes after mit, so you can say how you travel and understand the change.

deeper.text: One small word does two jobs. mit means with and also by (vehicle). mit dem Chef is with the boss, mit dem Zug is by train. German does not have a separate word for by here. You say with the train, and it is always followed by the dative.

cards.title: Masculine: der becomes dem
cards.body: A der-word after mit: der becomes dem. The noun itself does not change. Learn: der → dem. The m is the signal for the dative.

examples.en: I am talking to the boss.

examples.de: Leon fährt mit dem Zug nach Berlin.
examples.en: Leon goes to Berlin by train.

cards.more: Masculine words already changed once: der → den for the object. Now a second change: der → dem after mit. Do not mix them up: den has an n, dem has an m. A trick: m for mit, m for dem. Step 1: is the noun a der-word? Step 2: after mit, say dem. Step 3: keep the noun the same. Extra example: Ich telefoniere mit dem Arzt. = I am on the phone with the doctor.
cards.lead: You know that mit changes the article. Next: the masculine der-words after mit, so you can say who or what you work with, like the boss or the laptop.

deeper.text: Here is a memory trick: mit and dem both have an m. The m in dem is the dative signal, and mit is the word that asks for it. When you see mit, listen for the m in the next word. For masculine nouns it is always dem.

cards.title: Neuter: das becomes dem, too
cards.body: A das-word after mit also takes dem. So masculine and neuter look the same in the dative. That makes it easier: der and das both become dem.

examples.de: Frau Weber arbeitet mit dem Team.
examples.en: Frau Weber works with the team.

cards.more: Think of der and das as twins. In the dative they wear the same shirt: dem. So you only need to ask: is it die? If not, and it is one thing, the answer is dem. Step 1: find the article. Step 2: der or das? Say dem. Step 3: keep the noun. Extra example: Ben fährt mit dem Motorrad. = Ben goes by motorbike. (das Motorrad.)
cards.lead: You just saw the masculine change. Next: the das-words after mit, so you can say you go by car or play with a child.

deeper.text: Masculine and neuter share the dative form dem, and this pair stays together in other dative words too. Later you will meet einem the same way. Only feminine and plural look different. So you only need to remember three forms, not four: dem, der, den.

cards.title: Feminine: die becomes der
cards.body: A die-word after mit takes der. This one is a trap: der looks like the masculine word, but here it is the dative of die. die → der after mit.

examples.en: I am talking to the (female) boss.
Leon is on the phone with the customer.

cards.more: This is the one that tricks everyone. der usually means a masculine word. But after mit, a feminine word also says der. How do you know which? Look at the noun: die Chefin is feminine, so mit der Chefin is the dative. Step 1: is the noun a die-word? Step 2: after mit, say der. Step 3: keep the noun. Extra example: Ich fahre mit der S-Bahn. = I go by S-Bahn (city train).
cards.lead: Masculine and neuter both use dem now. Next: the die-words after mit, so you can say you talk with a female boss or take the tram.

deeper.text: A helpful clue: nouns ending in -in are always feminine, like Chefin and Kundin. So after mit they take der. When you read der Kundin, the ending -in tells you it is the dative of die, not a masculine der. The noun gives you the hint.

cards.title: Plural: den, and the noun adds -n
cards.body: Many things after mit: die becomes den. And the noun gets an extra -n at the end. If the plural already ends in -n, or ends in -s, add nothing.
steps: die Kinder (plural)
after mit: die → den
the noun adds -n: Kinder → Kindern
= mit den Kindern
but: mit den Kollegen (already -n), mit den Autos (-s: no n)
cards.more: The plural dative has two signals, like a belt and braces: den in front and -n at the end. Step 1: make the plural: die Freunde. Step 2: die becomes den. Step 3: does the plural end in -n already? Then stop. Does it end in -s, like Autos? Then stop. Otherwise add -n: den Freunden. Extra example: Leon fährt mit den Freunden nach Hamburg. = Leon goes to Hamburg with the friends.
cards.lead: You can handle one person or thing after mit. Next: the plural form, so you can say you play with the children or eat with your colleagues.

deeper.text: The extra -n is part of the dative plural rule: a plural noun in the dative ends in -n. Plurals that already end in -n need nothing. Plurals ending in -s also keep their ending, like Autos. Say it aloud once: mit den Kindern, mit den Autos.

cards.title: The three cases side by side
cards.body: Here is the whole table so far. Nominative = subject. Accusative = object, and after für. Dative = after mit. Look at the dative row: dem, der, dem, den.

examples.en: I am talking to the boss.

cards.more: Picture three rows of boxes, one row per job. Row 1, nominative: the doer. Row 2, accusative: the thing done to; only the masculine box changes. Row 3, dative: after mit; every box changes. Step 1: find the job: subject, object or after mit? Step 2: find the gender. Step 3: read the box. Memory line for row 3: dem, der, dem, den. Say it like a little song. Extra example: Die Chefin ist hier. Ich sehe die Chefin. Ich spreche mit der Chefin.
cards.lead: Now you have the forms for mit. Here they sit next to the other two cases, so you can see which job each case does in a sentence.

deeper.text: Look at the accusative row once more. Only masculine changes there: der becomes den. Feminine, neuter and plural stay the same as in the nominative. So the accusative is the easy case. The dative is the one that changes almost everything.

cards.title: Mit wem? With whom? In 3 steps
cards.body: Ask Mit wem? (with whom?). wem is the dative of wer. Answer with mit + dative, or with a name: names need no article. Mit wem arbeitest du? – Mit Frau Weber.

examples.de: Mit Mira fahre ich nach Hause.

steps: 1. Is there mit? → dative.
2. der, die, das or plural?
3. der/das → dem, die → der, plural → den + -n.
Mit wem? – Mit der Chefin.
cards.more: wer, wen, wem: the same person question in three outfits. wer asks for the subject, wen for the object, wem after mit. Step 1: ask Mit wem …? Step 2: the verb is on chair 2. Step 3: answer with mit + dative. A name is easy: no article, so nothing changes. Extra example: Mit wem telefonierst du? – Mit der Kundin. = Who are you on the phone with? – With the customer.
cards.lead: Last card of this lesson: asking Mit wem? with whom, so you can ask a colleague who they work with and answer with a name or a noun.

deeper.text: wem is the dative of wer. English once had this too: who and whom. English speakers mostly dropped whom, but German keeps the difference: wer is the subject, wen is the object, wem comes after mit. So Mit wem? is the only correct way to ask.

lessons.title: einem, einer, meinem: ein-words in the dative
lessons.goal: Use ein, kein and mein after mit, pay at the bank or shop, and tell the accusative from the dative.

grammar.point: ein-words (ein, kein, mein, dein …) take the same dative endings: -em for der and das, -er for die, -en + n for the plural
grammar.oneLine: mit einem Stift, mit einer Karte, mit meinem Kind, mit meinen Kindern.

mistake.why: mit always takes the dative. der Kugelschreiber is masculine, so ein becomes einem.

terms.meaning: ein, kein and the possessives (mein, dein, sein …): they all take the same endings
the end of the article after mit: -em (der, das), -er (die), -en (plural)
in cash, with coins and notes

cards.title: Before we start: einem, einer, meinem
cards.body: At the bank or the till you pay with a card or with a pen. After mit, ein and mein change too, just like der and die did. Today you do the same trick with ein-words.
steps: You already know: ein, kein, mein with the accusative (einen Hund, chapters 4 and 5), and mit dem (last lesson)
New today: ein, kein, mein, dein change after mit: einem, einer, einem, and plural -en plus n
By the end you can: say with what and with whom, like mit einem Stift or mit meiner Mutter

examples.why: You know this already. Here einen is the accusative.
New today: after mit, ein becomes einem.

examples.en: I am talking to my boss.
examples.why: New today: mein becomes meinem after mit.

cards.more: Last lesson der became dem. Now the same job for ein and mein: they get the same endings. Think of the endings as little stickers: -em for der and das words, -er for die words, -en for many things. Mein, dein and kein wear the same stickers as ein. You will also compare the dative with the accusative, so you can tell them apart. Step by step in the next cards.

cards.title: ein after mit: einem, einer, einem
cards.body: ein-words follow the same pattern as dem, der, dem. Just add the ending to ein: der-word → einem, die-word → einer, das-word → einem. Look at the last letters: -em, -er, -em, like dem, der, dem.

examples.en: Anna pays with a credit card.

cards.more: Look at the ends of the words. dem ends in -em, so einem ends in -em. der ends in -er, so einer ends in -er. The little ending is the same, ein is just glued in front. Step 1: find the gender. Step 2: take the ending from dem, der, dem. Step 3: glue it onto ein. Extra example: Ich telefoniere mit einer Kollegin. = I am on the phone with a colleague.
cards.lead: You can now change der and die after mit. Next: the same change for ein, so you can say you write with a pen or pay with a card.

deeper.text: Compare einen and einem. They differ by one letter, and the letter tells you the job: einen is the object of a verb, einem comes after mit. The same one-letter swap happens with dem and den. If you hear or read the m, think: after mit, so dative.

cards.title: mein, dein, kein: the same endings
cards.body: kein and the possessives (mein, dein, sein, ihr, unser, euer, Ihr) are ein-words. After mit they take the same endings: meinem, meiner, meinem. Careful: euer drops an e: eurem, eurer.

examples.en: I am talking to my boss.
Mira is on the phone with her mother.
Are you going in your car?

cards.more: You met this family in chapter 5: mein, dein and kein all copy ein. In the dative they still copy it. If you know einem, you know meinem, deinem and keinem. Step 1: pick the owner word: mein, dein, sein, ihr … Step 2: find the gender of the noun. Step 3: add -em, -er or -em. Extra example: Ben fährt mit seinem Bruder. = Ben goes with his brother.
cards.lead: The ein-words follow the same pattern. Next: my, your and no, with one trap in the word euer, so you can talk about your family after mit.

deeper.text: The ending of mein, dein and kein depends on the noun that follows, not on who owns it. A man says mit meiner Mutter, because Mutter is a die-word. Ben says mit seiner Mutter for the same reason. Look at the noun, then choose the ending.

example.en: Ben is on the phone with his mother.

cards.title: Plural: meinen … -n
cards.body: ein has no plural. But kein and the possessives do: they end in -en, and the noun adds -n, just like den Kindern. If the plural already ends in -n or -s, add nothing.
steps: meine Freunde (plural)
after mit: meine → meinen
the noun adds -n: Freunde → Freunden
= mit meinen Freunden
cards.more: The plural dative always has two signals: -en on the little word and -n on the noun. Step 1: make the plural: meine Kinder. Step 2: meine becomes meinen. Step 3: check the noun. Does it end in -n or -s already? Then stop. If not, add -n: Kindern. Extra example: Anna spricht mit ihren Eltern. = Anna talks to her parents. (Eltern already ends in -n.)
cards.lead: You know the singular endings for these words. Next: the plural form, so you can say you eat with your colleagues or play with your children.

deeper.text: Remember the n rule for plural nouns in the dative. Kollegen already ends in -n, so nothing is added: mit meinen Kollegen. Kinder has no -n yet, so it gets one: mit meinen Kindern. Check the last letter of the plural before you speak.

cards.title: At the bank and the till: paying
cards.body: You pay mit + dative: mit der Karte, mit einer Kreditkarte, mit dem Handy. Or you pay bar: in cash, with no mit. At the bank you have das Konto (account) and das Geld (money).

examples.de: Kann ich mit der Karte bezahlen?

cards.more: At the till the cashier often asks: Bar oder mit Karte? Cash or card? Step 1: decide how you pay. Step 2: cash? Say Ich bezahle bar. Step 3: card or phone? Use mit + dative: mit der Karte, mit dem Handy. Notice das Konto has a strange plural: die Konten. Many Germans still like to pay in cash. Extra example: Kann ich mit einer Kreditkarte bezahlen? = Can I pay with a credit card?
cards.lead: You can now name a thing after mit. Next: paying at the bank and the till, so you can say you pay by card, by phone or in cash.

deeper.text: In shop talk people often drop the article: Ich zahle mit Karte. Both mit der Karte and mit Karte are fine. zahlen and bezahlen mean the same, and zahlen is shorter and very common at the till. You will hear the short form every day in shops.

cards.title: Media: letters, parcels, messages
cards.body: Office and media words. Use them with the verbs you know: schreiben, lesen, schicken. die Nachricht is a message, die Zeitung a newspaper, die Zeitschrift a magazine.

examples.de: Mira schickt ein Paket mit der Post.
examples.en: Mira sends a parcel by post.
examples.why: Object ein Paket; mit der Post = dative.

examples.de: Leon liest die Zeitung im Internet.
examples.en: Leon reads the newspaper on the internet.
examples.why: im Internet: one piece for now.

cards.more: Notice how one sentence can hold two cases. In Mira schickt ein Paket mit der Post, the parcel is the object: accusative. The post comes after mit: dative. Step 1: find the thing being sent or read: that is the object. Step 2: find mit: the word after it is dative. im Internet is a piece for now; you will see why it is im in lesson 7. Extra example: Ich lese eine Nachricht. = I am reading a message.
cards.lead: Next: words for letters, parcels and messages, so you can say what you write, read and send at work with the verbs you know.

deeper.text: A handy pattern: nouns ending in -ung are always feminine. Zeitung is die, and so is Besprechung. When a new noun ends in -ung, you know its article without checking. That also tells you the dative: mit der Zeitung, not mit dem.

cards.title: Accusative or dative? Compare
cards.body: The object of a verb, and anything after für, is accusative: einen, den. Anything after mit is dative: einem, dem. Same noun, different job, different form.

examples.de: Das Geschenk ist für den Chef, und ich spreche mit dem Chef.
examples.en: The present is for the boss, and I talk to the boss.

cards.more: Think of two different doors. The für door and the object door lead to the accusative room: only masculine changes there (den, einen). The mit door leads to the dative room: everything changes (dem, der, dem, den). Step 1: is there mit? Dative. Step 2: is there für, or is it the thing you buy, see or have? Accusative. Step 3: is it the doer? Nominative. Extra example: Ich besuche meine Chefin. Ich spreche mit meiner Chefin.
cards.lead: You have a new job for these forms. Next: the difference between the object of a verb and the word after mit, so you can pick the right form in each sentence.

deeper.text: Many mistakes come from picking the form before asking the job. Make it a habit: look at the little word first. If you see mit, the dative follows. A verb like kaufen or sehen gives the accusative. Only then choose the ending.

cards.title: Choose the form in 3 steps
cards.body: Use these three questions every time. 1. What is the job: subject, object, or after mit? 2. What is the gender? 3. the-word or a-word? Then read the box in the table.
steps: 1. Job? subject → nominative, object or für → accusative, mit → dative
2. Gender? der, die, das or plural
3. the or a? dem / einem, der / einer …
mit + die Kollegin + a → mit einer Kollegin
cards.more: This is a small checklist, like checking your pockets before you leave: keys, phone, wallet. Step 1: find the job of the noun group. Step 2: find its gender. Step 3: pick the word for the or a. Do it slowly at first. After a week it becomes automatic. Extra example: Der Brief ist für eine Kollegin. = The letter is for a colleague. (für → accusative: eine stays.)
cards.lead: Last card of this lesson: three questions to check any ein-word, so you can pick the right form for any sentence in a few seconds.

deeper.text: Say the three steps aloud at first, slowly. After a week you will do them silently, in about a second. This is how fluent speakers also work, they just do it so fast they do not notice. Step 1 matters most: find the little word.

lessons.title: zum Arzt, beim Arzt: zu and bei + dative
lessons.goal: Say where you are going (zu) and where you are (bei), and understand zum, zur and beim.

grammar.point: zu (to: going) and bei (at: being there) always take the dative; zu + dem = zum, zu + der = zur, bei + dem = beim
grammar.oneLine: Ich gehe zum Arzt. Ich bin beim Arzt. Ich fahre zur Arbeit.

mistake.why: zu is for going somewhere (wohin?). To say where you are (wo?), use bei: bei + dem = beim.

terms.meaning: two words squeezed into one: zu + dem = zum, bei + dem = beim
where to? asks for the goal of a movement
where? asks for the place where someone or something is

cards.title: Before we start: zum Arzt, beim Arzt
cards.body: You feel ill and tell a friend: I am going to the doctor. Or you say: I am at the doctor. Two little words, zu and bei, do these jobs. You already used zum in chapter 3, now you see why.
steps: You already know: zum in Wie komme ich zum Rathaus? (chapter 3), and mit dem (this chapter)
New today: zu and bei take the dative: zu + dem = zum, zu + der = zur, bei + dem = beim
By the end you can: say where you go and where you are, like Ich gehe zum Arzt and Ich bin beim Arzt

examples.en: How do I get to the town hall?
examples.why: You know this already. You learned zum as one piece.

examples.en: I am going to the doctor.
examples.why: New today: zu + dem melts into zum. You are going there.

cards.more: Some words melt together, like do not becomes don't in English. Zu + dem melts into zum, and zu + der into zur. You have been saying zum Bahnhof and zum Frühstück already. Today you see the secret behind it: zu and dem. The other word, bei, means at: you are there, you are not going. Going is zu, being is bei. You will learn this step by step in the next cards.

cards.title: zu = to, always with the dative
cards.body: zu means to: you go to a person or a place. Like mit, zu always takes the dative. With a name there is no article: zu Anna. With mein, dein …: zu meiner Chefin, zu meinen Eltern.

examples.de: Am Sonntag fahre ich zu meinen Eltern.
examples.en: On Sunday I go to my parents'.

cards.more: zu is an arrow pointing at a goal. You move toward a person or a place. Like mit, it has a dress code: dative only. Step 1: you are moving toward someone? Use zu. Step 2: a name? Just say it. Step 3: a word with an article? Use the dative: meinem, meiner, meinen. Extra example: Leon fährt zu seinem Freund. = Leon goes to his friend's.
cards.lead: You now know the dative after mit. Next: zu, the word for going to a person or place, so you can say where you walk to.

deeper.text: The word zu has a second meaning that you will meet soon: too. Ich bin zu müde means I am too tired. It is the same word, but there is no dative and no noun after it, so you cannot confuse the two. Context makes it clear.

cards.title: zu + dem = zum, zu + der = zur
cards.body: Here is the secret of zum Bahnhof and zur Bank. zu + dem is always squeezed into zum. zu + der is squeezed into zur. So: der and das words → zum. die words → zur.

examples.en: I am going to the doctor.
How do I get to the town hall?

cards.more: Germans are lazy talkers, in a good way. zu dem is too long, so it melts into zum. zu der melts into zur. Step 1: find the gender. Step 2: der or das? Say zum. Step 3: die? Say zur. Plural does not melt: zu den. In chapter 3 you learned Wie komme ich zum Bahnhof? as a piece. Now you know: der Bahnhof, zu + dem, zum. Extra example: Ich gehe zur Post. = I am going to the post office.
cards.lead: You know zu takes the dative. Next: the melted forms zum and zur, so you can say you go to the doctor or to the town hall.

deeper.text: In everyday German you must say zum and zur. The long form zu dem sounds stressed, as if you mean that particular one. So never split them in normal speech. The pieces zum, zur, beim and vom are not optional shortcuts, they are the normal words.

cards.title: Old pieces, now explained
cards.body: You know these pieces already. Now you can see the dative inside them. zum Frühstück (das Frühstück), zum Geburtstag (der Geburtstag), zur Bank (die Bank). zu Hause and nach Hause stay fixed pieces with no article.

examples.de: Zum Frühstück esse ich ein Brötchen.
examples.en: For breakfast I eat a bread roll.

cards.more: It is like finally reading the recipe of a dish you have eaten for weeks. You said zum Frühstück and zum Geburtstag without knowing why. Now you can see the ingredients: zu + dem. Step 1: take the piece apart: zum = zu + dem. Step 2: find the noun's gender: das Frühstück. Step 3: das → dem, so zum. zu Hause is an old, frozen piece: keep it whole. Extra example: Zum Mittagessen esse ich Suppe. = For lunch I eat soup.
cards.lead: You have met zum and zur already. On this card: the old pieces you learned earlier, now with the reason behind them, so you can see the dative in each one.

deeper.text: zu is also used for occasions: zum Frühstück, zum Geburtstag, zum Essen. You use it for the moment something happens, as in for breakfast or for a birthday. This is why birthday greetings sound the way they do in German.

example.en: All the best for your birthday!

cards.title: bei = at: being at a place or with a person
cards.body: bei means at: at a person's home, at a shop or doctor, at a company. bei also always takes the dative. bei + dem is squeezed into beim. bei + der stays bei der.
cards.more: If zu is an arrow, bei is a pin on the map: you are already there. Step 1: are you at a place or with a person? Use bei. Step 2: der or das? Say beim. Step 3: die? Say bei der. Plural: bei den. A name: bei Mira, at Mira's place. bei a company means you work there: Ich arbeite bei einer Firma. Extra example: Heute bin ich bei Mira. = Today I am at Mira's.
cards.lead: Next: bei, which means at, so you can say you are at the doctor's or that you live with your parents.

deeper.text: bei Anna means at Anna's place. English has no little word for this, so you add 's. In German you just say bei and the name. It also works for firms and shops: bei der Post. You are inside the place or with that person.

cards.title: Going or being? zu or bei
cards.body: Ask wohin? (where to?) for movement: the answer uses zu. Ask wo? (where?) for a place: the answer uses bei. Same person or place, two little words.

examples.en: Where are you going? – To the hairdresser.
Where is Ben? – At the hairdresser's.

examples.de: Ich gehe zur Post, und dann bin ich bei Mira.
examples.en: I go to the post office, and then I am at Mira's.

cards.more: Picture a little film. Scene 1: you walk down the street. Where to? zum Arzt. Scene 2: you sit in the waiting room. Where? beim Arzt. Step 1: is someone moving? Ask wohin, use zu. Step 2: is someone already there? Ask wo, use bei. Step 3: both take the dative, so the article is dem, der, dem, den, and dem melts into zum or beim. Extra example: Ich gehe zum Zahnarzt. Jetzt bin ich beim Zahnarzt.
cards.lead: You know zu and bei. Next: wohin and wo, so you can tell whether someone is going somewhere or already there.

deeper.text: English often uses to or at for both ideas. German splits them cleanly: movement uses zu, being there uses bei. Ask yourself: is anybody travelling? If yes, wohin and zu. If not, wo and bei. Once you see the two questions, the choice is easy.

cards.title: Errands: places to go
cards.body: Errands are small jobs in town. Learn each place with its article, then make zu or bei: die Post, die Bibliothek (library), die Haltestelle (stop), das Amt (office of the city), die Praxis (a doctor's practice).

examples.en: I am going to the library.
We are walking to the stop.

examples.de: Morgen muss ich zum Amt gehen.
examples.en: Tomorrow I have to go to the city office.
examples.why: das Amt → zum; gehen at the end.

cards.more: Make a to-do list for a busy day. Every line is zu + a place. Step 1: write the place with its article: die Post. Step 2: turn it into zu: die → zur. Step 3: add the verb: Ich gehe zur Post. Inside a building like a library you will use in, not bei: that comes in lesson 7. If you use a modal like muss, the verb gehen goes to the end. Extra example: Zuerst gehe ich zur Post, und dann gehe ich zum Friseur. = First I go to the post office, and then I go to the hairdresser.
cards.lead: Last card of this lesson: errands in town, so you can say where you go for post, books or the bus stop, and how to name each place.

deeper.text: Look at the place words. Many that end in -e or -ek are feminine: die Haltestelle, die Bibliothek. Words for people who work somewhere often end in -er or -eur and are masculine: der Friseur. This is not a perfect rule, but it gives you a good first guess.

example.en: Leon is going to the doctor's office.

lessons.title: aus dem Büro, vom Arzt: woher? and a short email
lessons.goal: Say where you come from with aus and von, and plan and write a short email.

grammar.point: aus (out of: a building, city, country) and von (from: a person, a place you were at) always take the dative; von + dem = vom
grammar.oneLine: Ich komme aus dem Büro. Ich komme vom Arzt. Die E-Mail ist von Frau Weber.

mistake.why: aus means out of a building, city or country. Coming back from a person, like a doctor, uses von: von + dem = vom.

terms.meaning: where from? asks for the starting point
the subject line of an email or letter
formal = polite, for Sie (Sehr geehrte …); informal = friendly, for du (Liebe …)

cards.title: Before we start: aus dem Büro, vom Arzt
cards.body: You come back from lunch and a colleague asks: where do you come from? You can say Ich komme aus dem Büro or Ich komme vom Arzt. Today you learn the two little words aus and von and a short email.
steps: You already know: Ich komme aus Wien (chapter 1), and dem and der after mit (this chapter)
New today: aus and von take the dative: aus dem Büro, vom Arzt (von + dem = vom)
By the end you can: say where you come from, and write a short email

examples.en: I am coming out of the office.
examples.why: New today: aus is followed by dem, because Büro is a das-word.

examples.en: I am coming from the doctor's.
examples.why: New today: von + dem melts into vom.

cards.more: Think of a door. Aus is out of a building, a city or a country: you walk out of it. Von is from a person or from a place you visited. Both are followed by the dative, the same costume you met with mit, zu and bei. The little words dem and der are your old friends now. You will also practise a short email. Step by step in the next cards.

cards.title: aus = out of, with the dative
cards.body: You know aus from chapter 1: Ich komme aus Spanien. aus means out of: a country, a city, a building. Like mit and zu, aus always takes the dative. Most countries have no article. With a building: aus dem Büro.

examples.en: I am coming out of the office.
Mira is coming out of the canteen.

examples.de: Herr Ali kommt aus der Schweiz.
examples.why: die Schweiz has an article: aus der Schweiz.

cards.more: Picture a door. aus is you stepping out through it: out of the office, out of the canteen, out of a country. Step 1: you come out of a place? Use aus. Step 2: no article, like Spanien? Nothing changes. Step 3: an article? Dative: dem, der, dem, den. A few countries have an article. die Schweiz is one: aus der Schweiz. Extra example: Leon kommt aus dem Kino. = Leon is coming out of the cinema.
cards.lead: You know zu and bei with the dative. Next: aus, which means out of, so you can say where you come from or come out of.

deeper.text: aus carries the idea of being inside something first and then coming out. That fits a building, but also a city or country, where you are from. Most countries have no article. A few do, like die Schweiz, and those take der: aus der Schweiz.

example.en: Anna is coming out of the office.

cards.title: von = from, and von + dem = vom
cards.body: von means from: from a person, or back from a place where you were. von also takes the dative. von + dem is squeezed into vom. von + der stays von der.

examples.en: I am coming from the doctor's.

examples.de: Das Paket ist von meiner Mutter.
examples.en: The parcel is from my mother.

examples.de: Die E-Mail ist von Frau Weber.
examples.en: The email is from Frau Weber.

cards.more: You know von from chapter 5: von acht bis sechzehn Uhr. There it meant from a time. Here it means from a person or a place you visited. Step 1: is it from someone, or back from somewhere? Use von. Step 2: der or das? Say vom. Step 3: die? Say von der. Plural: von den. Extra example: Ich komme um fünf von der Arbeit. = I come from work at five.
cards.lead: You now have aus. Next: von, which means from a person or a place, so you can say a parcel is from your mother or that you come from the doctor.

deeper.text: von also shows who something belongs to, where English uses an apostrophe and s. German says the thing, then von, then the owner: das Auto von Ben is Ben's car. This is very common in everyday speech, and the owner after von is always dative.

example.de: Das ist das Auto von Ben.

cards.title: aus or von?
cards.body: aus = out of a building, a city or a country. von = from a person, or back from a place you went to (the doctor, work, the post office). For people, always von.

examples.en: Anna is coming from the post office.

cards.more: Ask yourself: was I inside it? Out of a building, a city or a country: aus. Back from a person or an appointment: von. Step 1: is it a person? Always von. Step 2: is it a country or city? Always aus. Step 3: a building you step out of? aus. An errand you come back from? von. Do not worry if you mix them sometimes: people will still understand you. Extra example: Die Nachricht ist von Leon. = The message is from Leon.
cards.lead: You can say aus and von. On this card: how to choose between them, so you know when to talk about a place and when about a person.

deeper.text: A good test: if it is a person, use von. A person is never a place you come out of. For places, aus tells you your origin, like aus Berlin, which means you are from there. von a place says you were just there and are coming back.

cards.title: Three questions: wohin, wo, woher
cards.body: Now you have a full set. wohin? (going) → zu. wo? (being there) → bei. woher? (coming from) → von or aus. All of them take the dative.

examples.en: Where are you going? – To the doctor.
Where are you? – At the doctor's.
Where are you coming from? – From the doctor's.

cards.more: Imagine a trip in three photos. Photo 1: you walk to the doctor: zum Arzt. Photo 2: you sit in the doctor's room: beim Arzt. Photo 3: you walk home from the doctor: vom Arzt. Step 1: pick the photo: going, being, coming. Step 2: pick the little word: zu, bei, von. Step 3: der or das melts: zum, beim, vom. die stays: zur, bei der, von der. Extra example: Wohin fährst du? – Zur Arbeit. Woher kommst du? – Von der Arbeit.
cards.lead: You have the forms for going, being and coming from. Next: the three question words, so you can ask and answer where someone goes, is or comes from.

deeper.text: Look inside the question words: wo + hin, wo + her. hin means away from the speaker and her means towards the speaker. So wohin asks where to, and woher asks where from. You can often split a word like this to see what it really means.

cards.title: Plan a short email in 4 steps
cards.body: Before you write, plan. 1. Betreff: the subject line. 2. Greeting. 3. Text: why you write, and one question or request. 4. Closing and your name. Keep the sentences short.

examples.en: Do you have time on Friday?

steps: 1. Betreff: Besprechung am Freitag
2. Liebe Anna,
3. am Freitag haben wir eine Besprechung. Hast du um zehn Uhr Zeit?
4. Viele Grüße / Ben
cards.more: An email is like a sandwich. The bread on top is the greeting, the bread at the bottom is the closing, and the filling is your message. Step 1: write the Betreff, three or four words. Step 2: greet: Liebe for a woman, Lieber for a man (chapter 6). Step 3: say why you write and ask one thing. After the comma, the next line starts with a small letter. Step 4: close with Viele Grüße and your name. Extra example: Lieber Leon, kommst du morgen ins Büro? Viele Grüße, Mira
cards.lead: Next: planning a short email in four steps, so you can write a clear message to a colleague without getting lost.

deeper.text: After the greeting comma, German starts the first word of the text with a small letter: Liebe Anna, am Freitag haben wir … The greeting works like a comma in the middle of a sentence. Only nouns and names keep capitals. This is one of the little things that makes an email look correct.

example.de: Liebe Mira, am Montag habe ich Zeit.
example.en: Dear Mira, on Monday I have time.

cards.title: Polite emails: Sehr geehrte … and Mit freundlichen Grüßen
cards.body: For Sie, use formal pieces. Greeting: Sehr geehrte Frau Weber, / Sehr geehrter Herr Ali, (geehrt = honoured). Closing: Mit freundlichen Grüßen. Look: mit + dative plural, Grüße → Grüßen!
cards.more: Think of clothes again: a T-shirt for friends, a suit for the boss. Liebe and Viele Grüße are the T-shirt. Sehr geehrte and Mit freundlichen Grüßen are the suit. Step 1: du or Sie? Step 2: a woman or a man? geehrte for Frau, geehrter for Herr. Learn these two as pieces; the ending rule comes much later. Step 3: close with Mit freundlichen Grüßen. Spot the dative: mit + plural, so der Gruß, die Grüße, mit Grüßen. Extra example: Sehr geehrte Frau Weber, ich komme am Montag zurück. Mit freundlichen Grüßen, Leon
cards.lead: Last card of this lesson: a formal email to a Sie-person, so you can open and close a polite message at work with the right words.

deeper.text: If you do not know the name of the person, use Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren, which means dear ladies and gentlemen. It is the standard opening for a formal email to a company or office. Remember the comma at the end, and again a small letter at the start of your text.

lessons.title: im Büro, in der Kantine: in + dative for where
lessons.goal: Say where someone or something is in a building with in + dative, and tell im Kino from ins Kino.

grammar.point: For where (wo?), in takes the dative: in + dem = im, in der, in den + -n. For going into (wohin?), in takes the accusative: ins Kino, in den Park
grammar.oneLine: Wo? Ich bin im Büro, in der Kantine. Wohin? Ich gehe ins Büro.

mistake.why: You say where you are (wo?), so in takes the dative: in + dem = im.

terms.meaning: the place where someone or something is (answer to wo?)
the place someone goes to (answer to wohin?)
a little word like in that takes the dative for where and the accusative for where to

cards.title: Before we start: im Büro, in der Kantine
cards.body: A colleague calls: where are you? You answer: in the office, in the canteen. Today in gets the dative when you say where you are. You already know im Kino, ins Kino and in den Park.
steps: You already know: in Berlin and ins Kino (chapters 1 and 6)
New today: in + dative says where you are: in + dem = im, in der, and in den + n
By the end you can: say where you are in a building, and tell im Kino from ins Kino

examples.why: New today: in + dem melts into im.
New today: die Kantine becomes in der Kantine.

cards.more: In is a two-way word, like a door that can mean being inside or walking in. Being inside, the place where you stand, uses the dative: im Büro. Walking into, the direction, uses the accusative: ins Kino, in den Park. Same word, different question. Wo asks where you are, wohin asks where you are going. You will learn this step by step in the next cards.

cards.title: im Büro: in + dem = im
cards.body: Since lesson 1 you say im Büro. Here is why. To say where something is (wo?), in takes the dative. in + dem is squeezed into im. So: der-word and das-word → im.

examples.en: The children play in the park.
The printer is in the corridor.

cards.more: You have seen this melting trick three times now: zum, beim, vom. im is the fourth one. in dem is a mouthful, so it melts into im. Step 1: ask wo? Step 2: der or das word? Step 3: say im. Remember am Montag? That is the same trick: an + dem = am. Extra example: Leon ist im Büro. = Leon is in the office.
cards.lead: You can now use zu, bei, aus and von. Next: in, which means in or at a place, so you can say where something is in the building.

deeper.text: In everyday speech you say im, never in dem. English uses different little words here: in, at or on, as in at the office or on the internet. German often uses just one: in. So whenever you are inside a place, im or in der is a safe first guess.

cards.title: in der, in den + -n
cards.body: A die-word: in der. No melting. Plural: in den, and the noun adds -n, as always in the dative. In der Kantine was a piece in lesson 2. Now you know: die Kantine, dative der.

examples.de: Frau Weber ist in der Besprechung.
examples.en: Frau Weber is in the meeting.

examples.de: In den Räumen ist es ruhig.
examples.en: It is quiet in the rooms.

cards.more: The table is the same dative row you know: dem, der, dem, den. Put in in front and let dem melt. Step 1: is it a die-word? Say in der. Step 2: plural? Say in den and add -n to the noun if it does not end in -n or -s. Step 3: der or das? Say im. Extra example: Die Kollegen sind in der Küche. = The colleagues are in the kitchen.
cards.lead: You know im from the office. Next: the die-words and plurals with in, so you can say you eat in the canteen or sit in a meeting.

deeper.text: English says at a meeting, but German says in der Besprechung. A meeting, like a room, counts as a space you are inside. This is why in is so common: a place, an event or a group can all work like a container that you are in.

example.de: Die Kollegen sind in der Besprechung.
example.en: The colleagues are in the meeting.

cards.title: Old pieces, now explained
cards.body: Many pieces you learned hide in + dem: im Supermarkt, im Café, im Internet. Even time pieces: im Mai, im Sommer. And in der Kantine is in + der. You were using the dative all along!

examples.en: I buy bread in the supermarket.

examples.de: Leon liest die Zeitung im Internet.
examples.en: Leon reads the newspaper on the internet.

cards.more: It is like learning that the song you hum every day has words. You hummed im Supermarkt, im Mai, im Sommer. Now you know the words: in + dem. Step 1: take the piece apart: im = in + dem. Step 2: check the noun: der Mai, das Café. Step 3: der and das both give dem. That is why all months and seasons take im: they are all der-words. Extra example: Im Winter fahre ich mit der Straßenbahn. = In winter I go by tram.
cards.lead: You have used im and in der since early lessons. Next: the reason behind these pieces, so you can see the dative hiding in words like im Supermarkt.

deeper.text: All months and all seasons are masculine: der Mai, der Juli, der Sommer, der Winter. So they always give im, as in im Sommer. That is why you never have to look up their article. This is one of the few patterns in German that has no exceptions.

cards.title: im Kino or ins Kino? Being or going
cards.body: in is special: it can take two cases. Being there (wo?): dative, im Kino. Going in (wohin?): accusative, ins Kino (in + das), in den Park. That explains your chapter 6 pieces. zu, bei, aus, von and mit are always dative.

examples.en: We are going to the cinema.

examples.de: Ich gehe in den Park, und dann bin ich im Park.
examples.en: I go into the park, and then I am in the park.

cards.more: Picture a door again. Walking through the door is a movement: accusative, like an object you push. Standing inside the room is a place: dative. Step 1: ask: is someone moving into it, or already inside? Step 2: moving: ins, in den, in die. Step 3: inside: im, in der, im. Only in works like this in this chapter. All the other little words you met today stay dative every time. Extra example: Ich fahre in die Stadt. Jetzt bin ich in der Stadt.
cards.lead: Next: in with a movement, so you can tell being in a place from going into one, using im Kino and ins Kino.

deeper.text: To decide between im and ins, ask yourself: is something moving? Ich gehe ins Büro has a path: you enter. Ich bin im Büro has no path: you are simply there. Only a few little words work in both ways. Later you will meet more of them, in is the first.

cards.title: In the building: Wo ist …?
cards.body: Ask Wo ist …? and answer with in + dative. Floors: im Erdgeschoss (ground floor), in der ersten Etage (first floor). erste ends in -en here, like am ersten Mai.

examples.de: Wo ist der Aufzug? – Im Flur, links.
examples.en: Where is the lift? – In the corridor, on the left.
The toilet is on the ground floor.

cards.more: A new office building is a maze on your first day. You need one question: Wo ist …? Step 1: ask Wo ist der Aufzug? or Wo ist die Toilette? Step 2: the answer uses in + dative: im Flur, im Erdgeschoss, in der Abteilung. Step 3: add links or rechts for the side. In Germany, the ground floor is the Erdgeschoss, and the first floor is one floor up. Extra example: Die Treppe ist im Flur, rechts. = The stairs are in the corridor, on the right.
cards.lead: You can say where things are with in. Next: asking Wo ist …? and naming floors, so you can find the lift or the toilet in a building.

deeper.text: Floors are counted as in Britain. The ground floor is das Erdgeschoss, and the first Etage is one floor above it. The ending of zweite becomes -en after in der: in der zweiten Etage. Numbers like erste and zweite (first, second) behave like adjectives.

Bonus: a melted word tells you the gender. zur Haltestelle? Then it is die Haltestelle. Extra example: Am Montag bin ich beim Zahnarzt. = On Monday I am at the dentist's.
cards.lead: Last card of this lesson: the full table of melted words, so you can check zum, zur, beim, vom, im, am and ins at a glance.

deeper.text: Here is a quick way to read the table. The melted words ending in m (zum, vom, beim, im, am) hide dem. zur ends in r and hides der. ins ends in s and hides das. The last letter tells you the article that is hidden inside.

lessons.title: Können Sie bitte …? Polite requests at work
lessons.goal: Ask colleagues politely for something, and say yes, no and thank you.

grammar.point: A polite request is a yes/no question with können: Können Sie (or Kannst du) first, bitte after the person, the second verb at the very end
grammar.oneLine: Können Sie bitte das Fenster öffnen? Kannst du bitte den Plan ausdrucken?

mistake.wrong: Können Sie bitte öffnen das Fenster?
mistake.right: Können Sie bitte das Fenster öffnen?
mistake.why: With können, the second verb is an infinitive and goes to the very end. The object stays in the middle.

terms.meaning: asking someone politely to do something
a yes/no question with können + bitte; softer than a command
You're welcome (an answer to Danke)

cards.title: Before we start: polite requests at work
cards.body: At work you need a colleague to open the window or print a plan. You do not give an order, you ask politely. You already know können and the yes/no question, so this is easy.
steps: You already know: Kannst du Gitarre spielen? with können at the front (chapter 5)
New today: Können Sie bitte ...? is a polite request: the other verb goes to the end
By the end you can: ask a colleague politely for something, and say yes, no and thank you

examples.why: You know this already. Verb first, the other verb at the end.

examples.de: Können Sie bitte das Fenster öffnen?
examples.en: Could you open the window, please?
examples.why: New today: the same pattern, now a request with bitte.

cards.more: A request is a question dressed in nice clothes. You do not say Open the window! like a boss. You ask whether the other person can: Können Sie ...? Then you add bitte and say what you want. The second verb waits at the end, like a train at the last station. With a friend you say Kannst du, with several friends Könnt ihr. You will practise this step by step in the next cards.

cards.title: A request is a yes/no question with können
cards.body: To ask a colleague for help, make a yes/no question with können. Können Sie goes first. bitte comes right after Sie. The object sits in the middle, the infinitive goes to the end.

examples.de: Können Sie bitte das Fenster öffnen?
examples.en: Could you open the window, please?
examples.why: Können | Sie | bitte | das Fenster | öffnen.

examples.de: Können Sie bitte die Tür schließen?
examples.en: Could you close the door, please?

examples.de: Können Sie bitte den Brief unterschreiben?
examples.en: Could you sign the letter, please?

steps: Können
Können Sie
Können Sie bitte
Können Sie bitte das Fenster
Können Sie bitte das Fenster öffnen?
cards.more: A request is a question, not an order. You leave the other person room to say no, and that is why it is polite. Step 1: start with Können. Step 2: add Sie. Step 3: add bitte, the magic word. Step 4: put the thing in the middle: das Fenster. Step 5: the action goes last: öffnen. It is the same bracket as Kannst du Gitarre spielen? from chapter 5. Extra example: Können Sie bitte den Plan schicken? = Could you send the plan, please?
cards.lead: You can now name office tasks and talk about the day. Next: how to ask a colleague for help politely, so you can make a request without giving an order.

deeper.text: Think of a request as a frame. Können stands at the front, the infinitive stands at the very end, and everything else sits inside the frame. The longer the sentence gets, the further apart the two verbs are. This frame shape appears all through German, so it is worth getting used to now.

example.de: Können Sie bitte die Tür öffnen?
example.en: Could you open the door, please?

cards.title: du and ihr: Kannst du …? Könnt ihr …?
cards.body: With a friend or a close colleague, use du: Kannst du bitte …? With two or more: Könnt ihr bitte …? The rest stays the same: bitte after the person, the infinitive at the end.

examples.de: Kannst du bitte die Tür schließen?
examples.en: Can you close the door, please?

examples.de: Könnt ihr bitte um neun kommen?
examples.en: Can you (all) come at nine, please?

cards.more: Same sentence, three different people. Only the first word changes, to match the person: kannst for du, könnt for ihr, können for Sie. Step 1: who are you asking? A friend: du. A group of friends: ihr. Your boss or a stranger: Sie. Step 2: pick the form from the table. Step 3: build the rest as always. Extra example: Könnt ihr bitte morgen kommen? = Can you (all) come tomorrow, please?
cards.lead: You just made polite requests with Sie. Next: the du and ihr versions, so you can ask a friend or a group the same way.

deeper.text: Learn the verb forms as a small set: ich kann, du kannst, wir können, ihr könnt, Sie können. The a changes to ö in the wir, ihr and Sie forms. The du form ends in -st, and ich has no ending at all. The frame stays the same for every person, only the first verb changes.

example.en: Can you all speak slowly, please?

cards.title: Where does bitte go?
cards.body: bitte usually comes right after the person: Können Sie bitte …? If there is a small word like das or es, bitte can come after it: Können Sie das bitte wiederholen? Both are polite.
cards.more: bitte is like a cushion you put between the person and the job. It makes the request soft. Step 1: say the modal and the person. Step 2: put bitte next. Step 3: if you have a tiny word like das, it may slip in front of bitte. Both orders are fine. Step 4: the action goes last. These three requests save you in every German conversation: wiederholen, langsam sprechen, buchstabieren. Extra example: Kannst du das bitte wiederholen? = Can you repeat that, please?
cards.lead: You can ask with können. Next: where bitte goes in the sentence, so your request sounds friendly and natural.

deeper.text: A very useful short phrase: Wie bitte? It means Pardon? or Sorry, what did you say? Use it when you did not hear or understand something. It is polite, short, and every German speaker uses it. Here bitte does not mean please, it asks for a repeat.

cards.title: Request or command?
cards.body: In chapter 3 you learned the Sie command: Bringen Sie bitte den Brief zur Post! It is fine for clear instructions. A request with können is softer. At work, use the request with colleagues and the boss.

examples.de: Bringen Sie bitte den Brief zur Post!
examples.en: Please take the letter to the post office!
examples.why: Command: verb first, Sie, no question mark.

examples.de: Können Sie bitte den Brief zur Post bringen?
examples.en: Could you take the letter to the post office, please?
examples.why: Request: können first, bringen at the end.

examples.de: Kannst du bitte das Paket zum Chef bringen?
examples.en: Can you take the parcel to the boss, please?

rows: Können Sie bitte das Fenster öffnen?
Bringen Sie bitte den Brief zur Post!
Können Sie bitte den Brief zur Post bringen?
Rufen Sie bitte Frau Weber an!
Können Sie bitte Frau Weber anrufen?

cards.more: A command is like a road sign: clear and short. A request is like a friend asking a favour. Step 1: command: the verb goes first, then Sie, then the rest, and an exclamation mark. Step 2: request: Können first, then Sie, and the verb moves to the very end. Step 3: a separable verb like anrufen stays in one piece at the end of a request: anrufen. Extra example: Können Sie bitte Frau Weber anrufen? = Could you call Frau Weber, please?
cards.lead: You know the Sie command from chapter 3. Next: when a command is fine and when a softer request is better, so you can speak well with colleagues and the boss.

deeper.text: Notice what happens to the verb. In a command, the main verb is the first word: Öffnen Sie. In a request, that same verb moves to the end: Können Sie … öffnen? That is why the request sounds softer: the verb waits until the last moment, as if the speaker is asking carefully.

example.de: Können Sie bitte den Plan schicken?
example.en: Could you send the plan, please?

cards.title: Office jobs with a separable verb
cards.body: Many office jobs use a separable verb. After können, the verb stays in one piece at the end: ausdrucken (print out), anrufen (call), mitbringen (bring along).

examples.de: Können Sie bitte den Plan ausdrucken?
examples.en: Could you print out the plan, please?
examples.why: ausdrucken in one piece at the end.

examples.de: Kannst du bitte Herrn Ali anrufen?
examples.en: Can you call Herr Ali, please?
examples.why: Herr becomes Herrn as an object: learn it as a piece.
Without a modal: aus goes to the end.

cards.more: You learned in chapter 6: a separable verb splits when it is alone, but stays whole after a modal. Step 1: with können, put the whole verb at the end: ausdrucken. Step 2: in the answer without a modal, split it: Ich drucke den Plan aus. One more small thing: Herr changes to Herrn when he is the object. Learn Herrn Ali as a piece for now. Extra example: Kannst du bitte Anna anrufen? – Ja, ich rufe sie an.
cards.lead: You can make requests. Next: separable verbs after können, so you can ask for office jobs like printing out a plan or calling someone.

deeper.text: Separable verbs show their two halves in a statement: Ben ruft Mira an. The prefix an goes to the end. In a request with können, the verb is not split: it stays whole at the end, as in Kannst du Mira anrufen? So one verb, two shapes: split in a statement, whole after können.

cards.title: Say yes, say no, say thanks
cards.body: Yes: Ja, gern. / Natürlich. / Kein Problem. No, politely: Leider nicht, ich habe keine Zeit. Thanks: Danke! The answer: Bitte! or Gern geschehen. (You're welcome.)

examples.de: Können Sie bitte die Tür schließen? – Ja, natürlich.
examples.en: Could you close the door, please? – Yes, of course.

examples.de: Kannst du bitte Kaffee kochen? – Leider nicht, ich habe keine Zeit.
examples.en: Can you make coffee, please? – Sorry, no, I have no time.

cards.more: Every request needs an answer, like a ping needs a pong. Step 1: yes? Pick one: Ja, gern. Natürlich. Kein Problem. Step 2: no? Start with leider, so it sounds kind, and add a short reason. Step 3: when someone helps you, say Danke! Step 4: when someone thanks you, say Gern geschehen. Vielen Dank is a stronger thank you. Extra example: Können Sie das bitte kopieren? – Kein Problem! – Vielen Dank! – Gern geschehen.
cards.lead: Last card of this lesson: short answers to a request, so you can say yes, say no politely and thank someone for their help.

deeper.text: leider means unfortunately, and it softens a no. Germans like to say it when refusing, often with a short reason. Without leider, a plain nein can sound hard in an office. And gern means with pleasure, so Ja, gern is a warm yes that adds a little kindness.
