lessons.title: ja, nein, doch: small talk in the office, and s, sch, st, sp
lessons.goal: Answer negative questions with doch, make small talk with colleagues and say s, sch, st and sp well.

grammar.point: A normal yes/no question: ja or nein. A negative question (with nicht or kein): yes = doch, no = nein
grammar.oneLine: Hast du Zeit? – Ja. Hast du keine Zeit? – Doch, ich habe Zeit!

mistake.wrong: Hast du keine Zeit? – Ja, ich habe Zeit.
mistake.right: Hast du keine Zeit? – Doch, ich habe Zeit.
mistake.why: The question has kein in it. To say yes to a negative question, use doch, not ja.

terms.meaning: a yes/no question with nicht or kein in it: Kommst du nicht?
yes, after a negative question or to say the opposite of a negative sentence
a short, friendly chat about easy topics like the weekend or the weather

cards.title: Before we start: ja, nein, doch
cards.body: Chapter 7 ends with small talk at work. A colleague asks: Don't you have time? If you do, ja sounds confusing in English. German has a special word, doch, for yes to a no-question.
steps: You already know: ja and nein for yes/no questions (chapter 2)
New today: after a question with nicht or kein, yes is doch
By the end you can: answer a negative question, make small talk with colleagues and say s, sch, st, sp well

examples.de: Hast du heute Zeit? – Ja, ich habe Zeit.
examples.en: Do you have time today? – Yes, I have time.

examples.de: Hast du keine Zeit? – Doch, ich habe Zeit.
examples.en: Don't you have time? – Yes, I do have time.
examples.why: New today: the question has keine, so yes is doch.

cards.more: Imagine a friend says: You are not hungry? In English, yes can mean yes I am or yes I am not. German is clearer. If the question has a nicht or a kein in it and you want to say the opposite, you use doch. Think of doch as a loud, friendly no, you are wrong. You will learn this step by step in the next cards, and you will also practise the sounds s, sch, st and sp.

cards.title: Normal question: ja or nein
cards.body: You know this from chapter 2. A yes/no question starts with the verb. Answer ja or nein, then a full sentence if you like. Nothing new here, just the start point.

examples.de: Hast du heute Zeit? – Ja, ich habe Zeit.
examples.en: Do you have time today? – Yes, I have time.

examples.de: Kommst du mit? – Nein, ich komme nicht mit.
examples.en: Are you coming along? – No, I'm not coming.

cards.more: This is the easy case, a light switch with two positions: ja or nein. Step 1: hear the verb first: it is a yes/no question. Step 2: check: is there a nicht or kein in the question? No? Then it is a normal question. Step 3: answer ja or nein. Keep this card in mind: the next card changes one thing. Extra example: Arbeitest du heute? – Ja, bis fünf. = Are you working today? – Yes, until five.
cards.lead: You can make requests with können. Next: answering a normal yes or no question with ja or nein, so you can reply to a colleague in the office.

deeper.text: When someone offers you something, ja alone can sound blunt. Germans say Ja, bitte (yes, please) to accept and Nein, danke (no, thank you) to refuse. This is very common with food, drinks and help, and it is the natural answer to a question like Möchtest du Tee?

cards.title: Negative question: yes = doch
cards.body: Sometimes the question has nicht or kein in it: Hast du keine Zeit? To say yes, you have time, do not say ja. Say doch. To agree with the no, say nein.

examples.de: Hast du keine Zeit? – Doch, ich habe Zeit.
examples.en: Don't you have time? – Yes, I do have time.
examples.why: kein in the question: yes = doch.

examples.de: Kommst du nicht mit? – Doch, ich komme mit.
examples.en: Aren't you coming along? – Yes, I am coming.
examples.why: nicht in the question: yes = doch.

examples.de: Arbeitest du heute nicht? – Nein, heute habe ich frei.
examples.en: Aren't you working today? – No, today I'm off.

cards.more: English gets messy here: Don't you have time? – Yes. Yes I have, or yes I don't? German fixes this with one extra word. doch means: oh yes, I DO. It flips the no in the question. Step 1: spot nicht or kein in the question. Step 2: you want to say the opposite, the positive? Say doch. Step 3: you agree with the negative? Say nein. ja never answers a negative question. Extra example: Trinkst du keinen Kaffee? – Doch, gern! = Don't you drink coffee? – Oh yes, I do!
cards.lead: You know ja and nein. Next: doch, for when a question has nicht or kein in it, so you can say yes to a negative question.

deeper.text: English can confuse here: Don't you have time? Yes means I have time, but No could also mean I have time. German avoids the problem. nein always agrees with the negative, and doch always says the opposite. So the answer is never ambiguous, even when the question is tricky.

cards.title: doch: say the opposite
cards.body: doch also answers a negative statement when you disagree: Das ist nicht teuer. – Doch! (Yes, it is!). It sounds strong, so say it with a smile. Short answers are fine: Doch! or Doch, ist es.

examples.de: Der Drucker ist nicht laut. – Doch, er ist sehr laut!
examples.en: The printer isn't loud. – Yes, it is very loud!
examples.why: Disagree with a negative sentence: doch.

examples.de: Du hast keinen Laptop. – Doch, ich habe einen Laptop.
examples.en: You don't have a laptop. – Yes, I do have a laptop.

examples.de: Mira ist nicht da. – Doch, sie ist in der Kantine.
examples.en: Mira isn't here. – Yes, she is, she's in the canteen.

steps: Hear: nicht or kein?
Disagree? → Doch!
Agree? → Nein / Stimmt.
Normal question without nicht/kein? → Ja or Nein.
cards.more: doch is a little flip switch. Someone says no, and doch flips it to yes. Step 1: listen for nicht or kein. Step 2: if you think the opposite is true, say doch. Step 3: add the real sentence without nicht or kein. Careful: doch can sound like a correction, so use a friendly voice. Extra example: Ben kommt heute nicht. – Doch, er kommt um zehn. = Ben isn't coming today. – Yes, he is, he's coming at ten.
cards.lead: You now have doch for negative questions. Next: doch when you disagree with a negative sentence, so you can answer strongly, the way friends talk.

deeper.text: In speech, doch is stressed: you say DOCH with a little more energy. That is how people hear the disagreement. In writing, the exclamation mark does the same job. It is a strong word, so use a friendly tone, and a small smile helps.

cards.title: Small talk at work: easy topics
cards.body: In the office kitchen, Germans chat about easy topics: the weekend, the weather, food, holidays, the work week. Money and politics are not small talk. Greet at lunch with Mahlzeit! and say Schönes Wochenende! on Friday.

examples.en: Enjoy your lunch! Are you going to the canteen too?

examples.en: Have a nice weekend! – Thanks, you too!

cards.more: Small talk is the oil in the office machine: a minute of chat makes the day smoother. Step 1: pick an easy topic: weekend, weather, food. Step 2: ask a short question: Wie war dein Wochenende? Step 3: answer short and friendly and ask back: Und du? Mahlzeit is a funny word: it means meal, and colleagues say it to each other around lunchtime. Extra example: Wie war der Urlaub? – Super, danke! = How was the holiday? – Great, thanks!
cards.lead: Next: small talk topics in the office kitchen, so you can chat with colleagues about weekends, food and lunch.

deeper.text: A small step into the past: war is the past of ist. So Wie war dein Wochenende? asks how your weekend was, and Das Wetter war schön says the weather was nice. You do not need the whole past tense yet. Just learn war as the was of sein.

cards.title: How is the work? stressig, anstrengend, ruhig
cards.body: Describe your day with sein + adjective, no ending: Die Woche ist stressig (stressful). Die Arbeit ist anstrengend (tiring). Heute ist es ruhig. Join two ideas with aber or und.

examples.de: Die Woche ist stressig, aber das Team ist super.
examples.en: The week is stressful, but the team is great.

examples.de: Heute ist es ruhig, und ich habe um vier Feierabend.
examples.en: Today it's quiet, and I finish at four.

cards.more: You already know the recipe from chapter 3: thing + ist + adjective, and no ending on the adjective. Step 1: pick the thing: die Woche, die Arbeit, die Besprechung. Step 2: ist for now, war for the past. Step 3: the adjective at the end. Step 4: join a second idea with aber for a contrast or und for more. Extra example: Die Arbeit ist interessant, aber anstrengend. = The work is interesting, but tiring.
cards.lead: You can talk about your day. Next: describing work with sein and an adjective, so you can say the week is stressful or today is quiet.

deeper.text: A word like sehr (very) goes in front of the adjective, and nicht (not) too: sehr stressig, nicht toll. After sein the adjective keeps its basic form with no ending. Later you will see that adjectives in front of a noun do get endings, but here the plain form is correct.

cards.title: Sounds: s, sch, st, sp
cards.body: s before a vowel sounds like a soft buzz (z in zoo): Sie, sehen. sch sounds like English sh: Schreibtisch. At the start of a word or word part, st and sp sound like scht and schp: Straße, sprechen, Besprechung.

examples.why: Sie, sehen: soft buzz. sch = sh.
sp = schp in sprechen and Be-sprechung.

examples.de: Die Post ist in der Bahnhofstraße.
examples.en: The post office is in Bahnhofstraße (Station Street).
examples.why: Post: s + t at the end. Straße starts a word part: scht.

rows: start of a word or part

cards.more: Say the sounds out loud, like a little warm-up. Step 1: buzz like a bee for s before a vowel: Sie, sehen. Step 2: hush a baby for sch: Schreibtisch. Step 3: start of a word with st or sp? Hush, then t or p: scht-raße, schp-rechen. Step 4: st in the middle or at the end is plain s + t: Post, ist. A fun test: Besprechung. Be is a front part, so sprechung starts a word part: Be-schprechung. Extra example: spät, Stift, Schule: schp, scht, sch.
cards.lead: Last card of this lesson and of the chapter: the sounds s, sch, st and sp, so you can say words like Straße and Besprechung clearly.

deeper.text: The sound rule works on word parts too. In Bahnhofstraße the part Straße starts with st, so it sounds scht. In Besprechung the part Sprechung starts with sp, so it sounds schp. Look for where a part begins, not just the whole word, and you will pronounce more words well.

reading.title: Eine E-Mail an Herrn Ali
reading.text:
Betreff: Besprechung am Donnerstag

Sehr geehrter Herr Ali,

Frau Weber macht bis Mittwoch eine Dienstreise. Sie kommt am Donnerstag zurück. Die Besprechung mit dem Team ist am Donnerstag um zehn Uhr. Kommen Sie mit dem Zug oder mit dem Auto? Vom Bahnhof fahren Sie mit der Straßenbahn zur Haltestelle Rathaus. Von der Haltestelle gehen Sie dann fünf Minuten zu Fuß. Unser Büro ist neben der Post. Mittags essen wir mit den Kollegen in der Kantine. Sie können dort mit der Karte oder bar bezahlen. Bitte bringen Sie den Plan für das Projekt mit. Haben Sie noch Fragen? Dann rufen Sie mich bitte an. Meine Telefonnummer ist 040 556 23.

Mit freundlichen Grüßen
Mira
